problem: Most zero-shot object-goal navigation (ZS-OGN) methods assume a single floor, yet over half of HM3D/MP3D validation scenes are multi-floor; the only multi-floor method (MFNP) has one-way stair transitions, merged multi-floor maps, cannot detect downward stairs and uses heuristic floor switching. LLM planners also call the LLM at nearly every step, which is costly and slow.
motivation: Service robots must find objects in unseen multi-floor buildings without pre-built maps or retraining. About 65% (HM3D) and 73% (MP3D) of validation scenes are multi-floor, and about 28% (HM3D) and 15% (MP3D) of episodes have the goal on a different floor from the start, so single-floor methods have a hard ceiling. Greedy VLM frontier methods (VLFM) oscillate, while per-step LLM planning is too expensive, which motivates a hierarchical use of the LLM.
key_idea: Build per-floor BEV maps with stair-aware traversability and bidirectional stair topology online, and invoke an LLM only occasionally (floor-level then frontier-level decisions) on top of cheap VLM-based frontier ranking.
insight: Gains come from the architecture, not from stronger foundation models: swapping MFNP's models for BLIP-2+Qwen2.5 lowers MFNP to 55.8 SR, while ASCENT stays at 65.2-67.9 SR across model configurations. Removing the exploration cost map, cross-floor transition or coarse-to-fine reasoning each costs about 8-9 SR on HM3D. Cross-floor episodes show the effect most clearly: 33.3 SR vs 13.4 for MFNP and 0.4 for VLFM, and perception is the main remaining bottleneck (the ideal-detector variant reaches 49.8 SR on those episodes).
method: BEV maps: an Exploration Value Map (BLIP-2 semantic similarity plus an exp(-d) proximity bonus for frontiers within d_theta) and a Stair-Aware Obstacle Map that re-labels detected stairs as traversable, with blacklist/cache records of failed/successful transitions. The chosen frontier goes to a pretrained PointNav controller.

Stair detection: an object detector box is kept only if its confidence exceeds a threshold and the semantic-segmentation (RedNet) stair-pixel ratio exceeds a threshold. Downward stairs are inferred from depth values below -0.2 m, then verified with LOOK DOWN and approach.

Cross-floor transition: navigate to a stair frontier, then to a rolling waypoint 0.8 m ahead until exiting the far side. Recorded start/end points are reused on revisits, and a climb longer than T/10 steps triggers a reverse and marks the stair impassable. Maps are kept per floor (lists L_obs, L_val), avoiding overlap and allowing bidirectional revisits.

Coarse-grained assessment: each frontier's RGB view is turned into a scene description (Places365 room type plus RAM object tags). Frontiers are ranked by M_val, the top-k are cached, and visually redundant ones are filtered with SSIM.

Fine-grained decision: triggered only when all frontiers are farther than d_theta and at least k exist. Qwen2.5-7B first decides whether to switch floors (minimum T/10 steps between switches) using floor descriptions and floor priors, then picks the intra-floor frontier using room/object descriptions and room-object co-occurrence priors.
Statistical priors: floor-level goal distributions from the benchmark training episodes and area-level object-room co-occurrence from HM3D statistics, fed into the LLM prompts.
Recovery: replan for transient failures (detection failure, stuck on stair) and backtrack for fundamental errors (stair misidentification, wrong floor).

setting.backbone: BLIP-2 (semantic similarity), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (LLM reasoning), D-FINE + Grounding-DINO detectors, Mobile-SAM, RedNet, Places365, RAM, pretrained PointNav policy (all frozen)
setting.training_data: none (training-free); offline statistical priors extracted from benchmark training episodes
setting.action_space: discrete low-level: MOVE FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN LEFT/RIGHT 30°, LOOK UP/DOWN 30°, STOP; frontier waypoints executed by a pretrained PointNav policy; 500-step limit
setting.privileged: none at test time, except dataset-derived floor/area priors from training splits (the 'Ideal' detector variant uses GT perception and is reported separately)

numbers_note: Split is called 'val' since the paper says validation episodes (HM3D 2,000 episodes/20 scenes; MP3D 2,195/11 scenes) without unseen wording. Real-world results (12 trials-ish, SR 41.7, SPL 22.8) are not in a benchmark and are omitted.
results: On HM3D ASCENT reaches 65.4 SR / 33.5 SPL, beating MFNP (58.3/26.7) by +7.1 SR and +6.8 SPL. On MP3D it reaches 44.5 SR vs MFNP's 41.1. Versus ApexNav it trades SPL (-2.3 on HM3D) for +5.3 SR. It needs only 2.0-2.7 LLM calls per episode vs 35-149 for other LLM planners, and reaches 33.3 SR on different-floor episodes vs 13.4 for MFNP.
limitations: Sensitive to perception and stair geometry: it fails when visual stair appearance contradicts navmesh geometry (12.5% and 36.0% SR in the stress-test scenes), and it handles only normal stairs, not spiral or irregular ones.
Assumes a static environment; moving pedestrians degrade obstacle mapping. Uses dataset-derived priors, which give a moderate benefit (+3.3 SR) but tie it partly to benchmark statistics.
Real-world success is modest (41.7% overall SR; 25.0% for lower-floor tasks), and the LLM runs on a remote server.
